meta.title: High-Risk Roles
meta.attribution: Insider Threat Analyst Career Framework, insiderthreatanalyst.com
meta.scope_note: A starting register of roles whose access, trust and opportunity make insider risk more consequential. Role is one factor in insider risk, never a judgment about the people who hold the role. Sources are cited per role; where a source is copyrighted, this file cites control or practice numbers and paraphrases rather than reproducing text.

sources.title: Insider Threat Mitigation Guide (2026 edition)
sources.what_it_says: Program-building guide for critical infrastructure. The September 2026 update, as CISA announced it, adds material on access control, visitor screening, hybrid and remote work, and managing risk from adverse employee separations.
sources.confidence_note: Not read. cisa.gov refused automated access on 2026-11-07, so neither the guide nor CISA's page was opened. The edition and its new topics come from CISA's September 2026 announcement as relayed by trade press (ExecutiveGov, Infosecurity Magazine, ABA Banking Journal). Several outlets relaying one announcement count as one source.

sources.title: SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations (release 5.2.0)
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.what_it_says: PS-2 requires a risk designation for every organizational position, screening criteria for those positions, and review and update of the designations at a frequency the organization defines. PS-3 (screening and rescreening), PS-4 (termination), PS-5 (transfer), PS-6 (access agreements) and PS-7 (external personnel) follow from it. AC-2(13) disables accounts of individuals within an organization-defined time of discovering significant risks; AC-5 separation of duties; AC-6 least privilege, with AC-6(5) restricting privileged accounts, AC-6(7) reviewing privileges, AC-6(9) logging privileged functions. PM-12 is the insider threat program control.
sources.confidence_note: Control statements read on 2026-11-07 in NIST's own OSCAL catalog for release 5.2.0 (usnistgov/oscal-content on GitHub). The DOI resolves to the NIST PDF, which names it as the publication's address.

sources.title: 5 CFR 731.106, Designation of public trust positions and investigative requirements
sources.publisher: U.S. Office of Personnel Management (Code of Federal Regulations)
sources.what_it_says: Every covered federal position (competitive service, excepted service, career Senior Executive Service, and contractor and nonappropriated fund positions) is designated high, moderate or low risk by its potential for adverse impact on the efficiency or integrity of the service. High and moderate risk positions are public trust positions, which may involve policy making, major program responsibility, public safety and health, law enforcement, fiduciary responsibilities, access to or control of financial records, or significant risk of causing damage or realizing personal gain.
sources.confidence_note: Read on eCFR (ecfr.gov), current text, 2026-11-07.

sources.title: Position Designation System and Position Designation Tool
sources.publisher: U.S. Office of Personnel Management and Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency
sources.what_it_says: The federal method for turning a position's duties into a risk and sensitivity designation and an investigation level. A critical-sensitive or special-sensitive national security designation automatically confers high-risk public trust; noncritical-sensitive confers at least moderate risk.
sources.confidence_note: Read on opm.gov on 2026-11-06. opm.gov refused automated access on 2026-11-07, so this was not re-checked. The full Position Designation System document has never been retrieved for this page.

sources.title: DoD Manual 8140.03, Cyberspace Workforce Qualification and Management Program
sources.what_it_says: Tracks, per position, whether the position requires designation as an IT Privileged User, and per person whether that requirement is met. Requires cyberspace personnel to meet security and sensitivity levels commensurate with the position.
sources.confidence_note: Read on esd.whs.mil on 2026-11-06. esd.whs.mil refused automated access on 2026-11-07, so this was not re-checked, and no paragraph numbers are cited. The separate DoD IT privileged user memorandum has not been retrieved.

sources.title: CNSSD 504, Directive on Protecting National Security Systems from Insider Threat (with Annex C)
sources.what_it_says: Sets user activity monitoring requirements for national security systems. NITTF's technical page lists a 2016 version that adds Annex C, Privileged User and Privileged Access Controls. NITTF lists that version, dated 09/15/2016, among items "not available for public release"; the link goes to NITTF's listing, not the directive.
sources.confidence_note: NITTF technical page read 2026-11-07: it confirms the 2016 version, its Annex C title and that it is not available for public release. The directive's text could not be read, so none of its requirements are reflected here.

sources.title: National Insider Threat Policy and Minimum Standards for Executive Branch Insider Threat Programs (Presidential Memorandum)
sources.what_it_says: Requires executive branch programs to gather and analyze threat-related information, monitor employee use of classified networks, and train the workforce. Applies monitoring to everyone with access to classified networks rather than to a list of roles.
sources.confidence_note: Transmittal memorandum read on govinfo.gov 2026-11-07. The minimum standards annex itself was not re-read.

sources.title: Common Sense Guide to Mitigating Insider Threats, Seventh Edition
sources.publisher: Carnegie Mellon University Software Engineering Institute (CERT Division)
sources.what_it_says: Twenty-two best practices. The ones most tied to roles: Practice 1 (know and protect critical assets), Practice 6 (include insiders and trusted external entities in enterprise risk assessments), Practice 11 (stringent access controls and monitoring on privileged users), Practice 15 (separation of duties and least privilege) and Practice 20 (a comprehensive termination procedure).
sources.confidence_note: Title, date (September 7, 2022), the count of 22 practices and the five practice numbers and titles read 2026-11-07 on SEI's library page and SEI's own PDF. Copyright Carnegie Mellon University; the PDF may be reproduced externally only in its entirety, so it is cited by practice number only.

sources.title: Role-based security risk assessment (insider risk)
sources.publisher: National Protective Security Authority (NPSA), United Kingdom
sources.what_it_says: A six-step method: identify critical assets, identify threats by intent and capability, estimate likelihood and impact, check existing countermeasures, and propose proportionate new ones. Roles that enable a risk are noted against it so extra measures can be considered. Recommends reviewing the risk register at least annually, or sooner after a change in threat, a major incident, a change to critical assets or a new mitigation. Names five insider risk types: unauthorised disclosure, process corruption, facilitation of third-party access, physical sabotage, and IT or electronic sabotage.
sources.confidence_note: Web page and the Spring 2023 PDF guidance read on npsa.gov.uk on 2026-11-06, marked Crown Copyright 2023 with no Open Government Licence statement found. npsa.gov.uk refused automated access on 2026-11-07, so none of this was re-checked.

sources.title: Industry Letter: Absence from the Office as an Internal Control Safeguard
sources.publisher: New York State Department of Financial Services
sources.what_it_says: The closest thing to a regulator's role list found. DFS recommends that sensitive positions at a minimum include people who can change official books, records or transactions (or influence others to), people with privileged access to information systems including authority to alter them, and people in specialized higher-risk products. Each institution defines absence for its own operations, taking into account both physical and electronic access, and may use a tiered approach, for example allowing email while blocking ledger and transaction systems. Addressed to state-chartered banks, thrifts, credit unions and foreign bank branches.
sources.confidence_note: Read on dfs.ny.gov 2026-11-07.

sources.title: SR 96-37, Supervisory Guidance on Required Absences from Sensitive Positions
sources.publisher: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System
sources.what_it_says: Mandatory time away as an internal control, because most frauds and embezzlements require the wrongdoer's continual presence. Names trading and wire transfer as examples of sensitive key positions and asks each organization to assess its own significant risk areas. Duties are not to be performed physically or electronically during the absence.
sources.confidence_note: Read on federalreserve.gov 2026-11-07. The attachment was revised on October 1, 2025 to remove references to reputational risk.

sources.title: FFIEC IT Examination Handbook, Information Security booklet (July 2006)
sources.what_it_says: Personnel security section: the sensitivity of a job or access level may warrant additional background and credit checks; contractors should be subject to similar screening; managers should stay alert to changes in personal circumstances after hire. Superseded: FFIEC members issued a revised Information Security booklet on September 9, 2016. The revised booklet's personnel security language has not been checked for this page.
sources.confidence_note: The 2006 text was read on an archived copy on 2026-11-06; the archive host was not reachable on 2026-11-07, so it was not re-checked. The 2016 revision is confirmed from the FFIEC members' release as posted on ncua.gov (read 2026-11-07). The current booklet on ithandbook.ffiec.gov refused automated access, so its wording, and whether a later revision exists, were not checked.

sources.title: Section 205(d) of the Federal Credit Union Act and 12 CFR Part 752
sources.what_it_says: Generally prohibits people convicted of, or in a pretrial diversion program for, a crime involving dishonesty or breach of trust from working at or participating in the affairs of a federally insured credit union without NCUA consent. Amended by the Fair Hiring in Banking Act in 2022. Banks have a parallel rule in Section 19 of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act, which also covers money laundering offenses and requires the FDIC's prior written consent.
sources.confidence_note: Read on ncua.gov 2026-11-07. Section 19 read in the FDIC's copy of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act on fdic.gov the same day.

sources.title: 45 CFR 164.308, HIPAA Security Rule administrative safeguards
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (Code of Federal Regulations)
sources.what_it_says: Workforce security, with addressable implementation specifications: authorization and supervision of workforce members who work with ePHI, a workforce clearance procedure to determine that access is appropriate, termination procedures, information access management, and regular review of information system activity.
sources.confidence_note: Read on eCFR (ecfr.gov), current text, 2026-11-07.

sources.title: 21 CFR 1301.76, Other security controls for practitioners (controlled substances)
sources.publisher: Drug Enforcement Administration (Code of Federal Regulations)
sources.what_it_says: A registrant may not employ, in a role with access to controlled substances, a person convicted of a felony relating to controlled substances or whose DEA registration was denied, revoked or surrendered for cause. Theft or significant loss must be reported to DEA within one business day.
sources.confidence_note: Read on eCFR (ecfr.gov), current text, 2026-11-07.

sources.title: ISO/IEC 27002:2022 (and Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022)
sources.what_it_says: Relevant controls by number and title: 5.3 Segregation of duties; 5.18 Access rights; 5.19 Information security in supplier relationships; 6.1 Screening; 6.2 Terms and conditions of employment; 6.5 Responsibilities after termination or change of employment; 6.6 Confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements; 8.2 Privileged access rights; 8.16 Monitoring activities.
sources.confidence_note: Not checked against ISO. Control numbers and titles come from secondary mappings consulted on 2026-11-06; the standard is paywalled and iso.org refused automated access on 2026-11-07. Cited by number and title only.

sources.title: 2017 Trust Services Criteria (with revised points of focus, 2022), basis of SOC 2
sources.what_it_says: Cited for its logical access criteria, given here from general knowledge as CC6.1 to CC6.3 (access provisioning, removal, and role-based access designed around least privilege and segregation of duties). Not checked against the criteria text; cited by criterion ID only.
sources.confidence_note: AICPA's resource page for this document was read 2026-11-07 and confirms its title. The criteria document itself downloads only after signing in to an AICPA account, so it was not read. Check the criterion IDs and topics against it before relying on them.

sources.title: PCI DSS v4.0.1
sources.what_it_says: Requirement 12.7.1: people who will have access to the cardholder data environment are screened before hire, within local law. A third-party copy of the standard reports an applicability note that makes this a recommendation only for roles such as cashiers who see one card number at a time; that note has not been checked against the official text. Requirement 7 restricts access to cardholder data by business need to know.
sources.confidence_note: Requirement 12.7.1 wording matches third-party copies of the standard (checked again 2026-11-07); the cashier note was read on one such copy on 2026-11-06 only. The official v4.0.1 PDF was not retrieved: PCI SSC's direct document link answered that it must be opened from the document library. Paraphrased here.

sources.title: SP 800-181 Rev. 1, Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity (NICE Framework)
sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
sources.what_it_says: Describes cybersecurity work as work roles built from tasks, knowledge and skills. It describes the work, not the risk of the person doing it, so it does not rank roles. Useful for naming technical roles consistently; this site's KSA to NICE crosswalk is at /crosswalk.
sources.confidence_note: Read in the NIST PDF 2026-11-07: work roles are built from task, knowledge and skill statements. The site's crosswalk uses the same structure.

sources.title: Insider Threat TTP Knowledge Base
sources.what_it_says: Insider tactics, techniques and procedures built from incident data and ATT&CK. Organized by behavior, not by role, so it helps choose what to monitor for a role rather than which roles to designate.
sources.confidence_note: Read on GitHub 2026-11-07 (center-for-threat-informed-defense/insider-threat-ttp-kb): copyright 2024 Center for Threat-Informed Defense, Apache License 2.0; ATT&CK content inside it carries the separate ATT&CK terms of use. The ctid.mitre.org project page was not opened.

sources.title: The Insider Threat Matrix
sources.what_it_says: A framework of insider behaviors and the detections and preventions that map to them. Like the MITRE knowledge base it is organized by behavior, not role.
sources.confidence_note: License read on insiderthreatmatrix.org/terms-of-use 2026-11-07: Forscie grants a non-exclusive, royalty-free license for research, development and commercial use, provided copies carry Forscie's copyright notice and the license. This page links to the Matrix and reproduces none of it.

categories.name: Technology and privileged access
categories.summary: People who can change the systems everyone else depends on, including the logs and controls that would show what they did.

roles.name: System and network administrators

why.access: Administrative rights on servers, endpoints, network gear and backups, often across the whole estate.
why.trust: Trusted to act without per-action approval, frequently out of hours.
why.opportunity: Can create accounts, change configurations, disable logging and touch backups; sabotage and data theft both fit inside normal-looking work.
why.pressure: On-call load, layoffs and outsourcing hit this group; grievances about being undervalued are a recurring theme in IT sabotage cases.

indicators: Privileged sessions with no matching change ticket
New accounts, keys or scheduled tasks created outside the change process
Logging, EDR or backup jobs disabled or reconfigured
Unapproved remote-access tools or tunnels
Access to systems outside the person's assigned scope

controls.screening: Elevated pre-hire screening proportionate to the role, rescreening on promotion into wider admin scope.
controls.privileged_access: Separate admin accounts, just-in-time elevation, vaulted credentials, no standing domain-wide rights.
controls.separation_of_duties: No single admin can both change and approve production changes, or both administer and erase the logs that record them.
controls.monitoring: Session recording or command logging for privileged sessions, shipped to a log store the admin cannot alter.
controls.offboarding: Same-day revocation of every privileged credential, key and token; rotate shared secrets the person knew.

roles.name: Cloud, SaaS and identity administrators

why.access: Tenant-wide control of cloud accounts, identity providers, email and collaboration platforms.
why.trust: Can grant themselves or others access to almost anything, usually through a web console from anywhere.
why.opportunity: One role assignment, mailbox delegation or API token can expose an entire tenant; actions can look like routine administration.
why.pressure: Same pressures as other administrators, plus a high outside market value that makes them recruitment targets.

typical_access: Identity provider global or privileged role administrator
Cloud organization owner or root account
indicators: Self-assigned or temporary role grants that are not removed
Mail forwarding rules, delegation or eDiscovery searches without a case
New OAuth apps, service principals or long-lived keys
Conditional-access or MFA policy exceptions
Console sign-ins from unusual locations or devices

controls.screening: As for system administrators.
controls.privileged_access: Privileged identity management with time-bound, approved activation; break-glass accounts sealed and alerted on.
controls.separation_of_duties: Role assignment and policy changes for privileged roles require a second approver.
controls.monitoring: Tenant audit logs exported to a store outside the admins' control; alert on privileged role changes and mailbox access by admins.
controls.offboarding: Remove role assignments, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, and inventory keys and apps the person created.

roles.name: Developers and DevOps engineers with production access

why.access: Source code, build pipelines, deployment rights, secrets and sometimes production data.
why.trust: Code they write runs with the organization's authority, and review is often lighter than assumed.
why.opportunity: Logic bombs, backdoors, data exfiltration through code or pipelines, and theft of source code as intellectual property.
why.pressure: Departure to competitors, disputes over ownership of work, and layoffs.

typical_access: Copies of production data in lower environments
indicators: Commits that bypass review or land outside normal hours just before departure
Pipeline or branch-protection changes
Bulk cloning of repositories outside the person's projects
Secrets read that the person's services do not use
Production data copied to personal or unmanaged locations

controls.screening: Standard screening; elevated for engineers with standing production or secrets access.
controls.privileged_access: No standing production access; time-bound break-glass with approval and recording.
controls.separation_of_duties: Mandatory peer review and protected branches so no one ships alone; deploy rights separate from approve rights.
controls.monitoring: Repository, pipeline and secrets-access audit logs; watch for bulk clone and archive activity.
controls.offboarding: Revoke Git, cloud and pipeline credentials; rotate secrets the person could read; review their recent commits.

roles.name: Database administrators and data engineers

why.access: Direct access to the data itself, below the application controls that normally limit what a user sees.
why.trust: Expected to query, copy and move large datasets as part of the job.
why.opportunity: Bulk extraction of customer, financial or health records, and quiet alteration of records.
why.pressure: Data has a ready resale market; this role is an obvious target for outside recruitment.

indicators: Queries pulling full tables of sensitive fields with no matching request
New exports, replication targets or scheduled jobs to unfamiliar destinations
Direct edits to records that normally change only through applications
Database audit settings changed

controls.screening: Elevated screening where the data includes financial, health or other regulated records.
controls.privileged_access: Named accounts, not shared ones; just-in-time elevation to owner roles.
controls.separation_of_duties: Changes to production data through approved change paths, not ad hoc DML.
controls.monitoring: Database activity monitoring on sensitive tables, shipped off the database server.
controls.offboarding: Revoke database and pipeline access; review recent exports and jobs.

roles.name: Service accounts, automation and AI agents acting for someone

why.access: Often holds broader and longer-lived access than any person, because it was set up once and never revisited.
why.trust: Its actions are attributed to a system, not a person, so they draw less scrutiny.
why.opportunity: A person who controls the account or the agent's instructions can act through it; an agent can also act wrongly on its own.
why.pressure: Not applicable to the account; applies to whoever controls it.

typical_access: AI agents with tool or data access
indicators: Interactive sign-in by an account that should only run unattended
Agent or bot actions outside its defined task
Credential or prompt changes by someone who does not own the account

controls.screening: Not applicable; screen and record the human owner.
controls.privileged_access: Every non-human identity has a named human owner, least privilege, and an expiry.
controls.separation_of_duties: The person who builds an agent or bot does not alone approve its permissions.
controls.monitoring: Log agent and service actions with the owning human recorded; see A-AGENT01 in the framework.
controls.offboarding: When an owner leaves, reassign or disable their service accounts and agents the same day.

categories.name: Security and oversight functions
categories.summary: The people who watch everyone else. They need the same controls, applied by someone outside their own chain.

roles.name: SOC, insider risk and investigations analysts

why.access: Monitoring data about everyone: user activity, email, HR case notes, investigation files.
why.trust: Trusted to look at sensitive information about colleagues and to keep it confidential.
why.opportunity: Curiosity lookups, leaking an investigation, tipping off a subject, or tuning detections to blind the tooling.
why.pressure: Exposure to distressing material, workload and moral injury; see the Wellness page.

indicators: Searches on colleagues with no open case or tasking
Exports of case material
Detection rules, exclusions or allow-lists changed without review
Alerts about the analyst's own activity closed by the analyst

controls.screening: Elevated screening and periodic rescreening, as for other privileged roles.
controls.privileged_access: Access tied to assigned cases; no standing access to every subject's data.
controls.separation_of_duties: No analyst reviews alerts on themselves or their own team; detection changes reviewed by a second person.
controls.monitoring: Audit the auditors: a separate function reviews analyst queries and case access.
controls.offboarding: Immediate removal from tools and cases; hand off open investigations under supervision.

roles.name: Legal, compliance, internal audit and ethics staff

why.access: Privileged legal material, regulatory correspondence, audit findings, whistleblower reports, M&A plans.
why.trust: Often have broad read access by design so they can test or advise anywhere.
why.opportunity: Leaking privileged or market-moving information, suppressing findings, or trading on what they know.
why.pressure: Conflicts between loyalty and duty, and outside interest in what they hold.

indicators: Access to matters outside the person's assignments
Downloads of deal or regulatory material near personal trading windows
Findings or hotline cases closed without the normal review

controls.screening: Standard screening; elevated for staff on market-sensitive deals.
controls.privileged_access: Matter-based access and ethical walls rather than blanket read rights.
controls.separation_of_duties: Findings and hotline closures need a second reviewer; auditors do not audit work they performed.
controls.monitoring: Monitor access to deal rooms and hotline data; pair with personal trading pre-clearance where relevant.
controls.offboarding: Revoke matter access and remind of continuing confidentiality obligations.

categories.name: Money movement and finance
categories.summary: Roles that can move, record or approve money. Regulators have treated these as sensitive positions for decades.

roles.name: Wire, payments and treasury staff

why.access: Can initiate, approve or release funds transfers and change beneficiary details.
why.trust: Trusted with large sums and urgent requests.
why.opportunity: Fraudulent transfers, beneficiary changes, or collusion with outside fraudsters, including business email compromise.
why.pressure: Personal financial strain, gambling, or coercion by outside criminals.

typical_access: Beneficiary and vendor bank detail records
indicators: Transfers just under approval thresholds
Beneficiary changes followed quickly by payments
Overrides of callback or verification steps
Reluctance to take leave or let others cover the desk

controls.screening: Elevated screening including credit history where lawful; rescreen on promotion to approver.
controls.privileged_access: Payment entitlements by role, reviewed at least quarterly.
controls.separation_of_duties: Dual control: one person initiates, another approves, and beneficiary changes are verified out of band.
controls.monitoring: Payment anomaly monitoring and review of overrides; mandatory time away with no system access.
controls.offboarding: Remove payment entitlements and tokens before notice is announced where practical.

roles.name: Accounts payable, receivable and general ledger staff

why.access: Vendor master data, invoices, journal entries and reconciliations.
why.trust: Trusted to keep the books accurate with limited line-by-line review.
why.opportunity: Fictitious vendors, invoice and refund schemes, and journal entries that hide losses.
why.pressure: Personal financial pressure; pressure to hit targets.

typical_access: ERP accounts payable and receivable modules
indicators: Vendors created and paid by the same person
Vendor bank details matching employee details
Manual journal entries near period end without support
Reconciliations always done by one person who resists help

controls.screening: Standard screening; elevated where the role can both create and pay vendors.
controls.privileged_access: Restrict vendor master changes to a small group outside AP.
controls.separation_of_duties: Separate vendor setup, invoice entry, payment approval and reconciliation.
controls.monitoring: Vendor-employee data matching and journal entry analytics.
controls.offboarding: Revoke ERP roles and review the person's recent vendor and journal activity.

categories.name: People data
categories.summary: Roles that hold information about everyone else, including the information an insider risk program depends on.

roles.name: HR, payroll and benefits staff

why.access: Personal data on the whole workforce: identity documents, salaries, bank details, medical and disciplinary records.
why.trust: Trusted with confidential employee matters, including upcoming terminations and investigations.
why.opportunity: Ghost employees, pay changes, identity theft, leaking terminations or tipping off a subject.
why.pressure: Exposure to conflict and difficult cases; personal relationships with affected staff.

indicators: Pay or bank detail changes made and approved by the same person
Records viewed for employees outside the person's client group
Employees added without a matching requisition
Early knowledge of terminations showing up elsewhere

controls.screening: Elevated screening for payroll and employee relations roles.
controls.privileged_access: Field-level access so most HR staff cannot see bank details or medical records.
controls.separation_of_duties: Payroll changes entered by one person and approved by another; new hires reconciled to requisitions.
controls.monitoring: Audit access to sensitive HR records and payroll changes.
controls.offboarding: Revoke HRIS access promptly; HR staff are also the people who start everyone else's offboarding, so plan who starts theirs.

categories.name: Leadership and the people around them
categories.summary: Authority, not technical access, is what makes these roles high consequence.

roles.name: Executives and board members

why.access: Strategy, M&A, financial results, and authority to approve exceptions.
why.trust: Rarely subject to the controls they approve for others.
why.opportunity: Overriding controls, insider trading, leaking strategy, or directing others to act improperly.
why.pressure: High stakes, public scrutiny, and targeting by foreign intelligence, activists and criminals.

indicators: Requests to bypass normal approvals for urgency
Exceptions granted to themselves or close associates
Unusual access to deal or results information outside their remit

controls.screening: Elevated screening at appointment, proportionate to role and law.
controls.privileged_access: Executives do not hold standing administrator rights.
controls.separation_of_duties: Exceptions and overrides by executives are logged and reviewed by the board or audit committee.
controls.monitoring: Governance oversight rather than routine activity monitoring; protect them as targets too.
controls.offboarding: Plan departures in advance, including board materials, devices and delegated access.

roles.name: Executive assistants and chiefs of staff

why.access: Delegated access to an executive's email, calendar, files and sometimes approval authority.
why.trust: Act on the executive's behalf every day; their actions look like the executive's.
why.opportunity: Leaking calendars and board material, approving in the executive's name, or being the route a social engineer uses.
why.pressure: Long hours, proximity to power without its rewards, and direct targeting by outsiders.

indicators: Delegated mailbox access used outside working patterns
Forwarding or sharing executive material externally
Approvals in the executive's name the executive does not recognize

controls.screening: Screen to the level of the executive they support.
controls.privileged_access: Scope delegation to what the job needs and review it when either person changes role.
controls.separation_of_duties: Assistants do not approve their own expenses or changes to their own access.
controls.monitoring: Audit delegated access to executive mailboxes and files.
controls.offboarding: Remove delegations the same day; tell the executive.

categories.name: Procurement and vendor management
categories.summary: Roles that decide who gets paid and who gets let in.

roles.name: Procurement and vendor management staff

why.access: Contract award, vendor onboarding, and often the decision to give a supplier access to systems or sites.
why.trust: Trusted to choose suppliers fairly.
why.opportunity: Kickbacks, bid rigging, conflicts of interest, and onboarding a supplier that then becomes an access path.
why.pressure: Outside inducements from suppliers.

indicators: Repeated awards to the same supplier without competition
Undisclosed relationships with suppliers
Supplier access approved without the normal risk review

controls.screening: Standard screening plus annual conflict-of-interest declarations.
controls.privileged_access: Separate the authority to award from the authority to grant supplier system access.
controls.separation_of_duties: Requisition, award, receipt and payment handled by different people.
controls.monitoring: Spend analytics and conflict-of-interest data matching.
controls.offboarding: Hand over open sourcing events under supervision.

categories.name: Physical security and facilities
categories.summary: Roles that control who and what gets into buildings, and can move unescorted where others cannot.

roles.name: Physical security, facilities and maintenance staff

why.access: Badge systems, keys, cameras, plant rooms, data centers and after-hours access.
why.trust: Trusted to be anywhere, at any time, often unescorted.
why.opportunity: Theft, sabotage, letting others in, or deleting camera footage.
why.pressure: Often lower-paid and contracted out, with less connection to the organization.

indicators: Badge rights granted outside the request process
Camera gaps or deleted footage
After-hours presence in areas unrelated to work orders
Tailgating or propping doors for others

controls.screening: Elevated screening for access-control administrators and staff with data center or vault access.
controls.privileged_access: Badge administration separate from badge request approval; key control logs.
controls.separation_of_duties: No one both grants and audits physical access.
controls.monitoring: Correlate badge, camera and work-order data; review access-control admin changes.
controls.offboarding: Recover badges and keys and re-key where needed; remove access-control admin rights.

categories.name: Contractors and third parties
categories.summary: Insiders by access, outsiders by employer. NPSA lists facilitation of third-party access as one of its five insider risk types.

roles.name: Contractors, consultants, MSPs and outsourced staff with standing access

why.access: Often the same system and site access as employees, sometimes more, through managed-service tooling.
why.trust: Trusted under a contract, but screened and supervised by someone else.
why.opportunity: Access that outlives the engagement, weak supervision, and shared accounts.
why.pressure: Short tenures, lower loyalty, and pressures the hiring organization cannot see.

typical_access: Remote management tools from the provider
Copies of data in the provider's environment
indicators: Access continuing after the engagement end date
Shared or generic accounts in use
Provider remote tools connecting outside agreed windows

controls.screening: Contract requires screening equivalent to employees in comparable roles, with evidence.
controls.privileged_access: Named accounts, time-bound, with an internal sponsor who reviews them.
controls.separation_of_duties: Contractors do not approve their own access or work.
controls.monitoring: Same monitoring scope as employees in the equivalent role, stated in the contract.
controls.offboarding: Provider must notify transfers and terminations within an agreed time; sponsor confirms removal.

categories.name: Transient high-risk states
categories.summary: Not roles but moments. Anyone can pass through them, and the risk attaches to the moment, not the person.

roles.name: Departing employees (resignation, notice period, termination, layoff)

why.access: Still holds full access while their attachment to the organization ends.
why.trust: Trust is often unchanged in systems even when the relationship has changed.
why.opportunity: Taking data, customer lists or code to the next job; sabotage after an adverse separation.
why.pressure: Grievance, financial worry, or a new employer's expectations.

typical_access: Whatever the person held in their role
indicators: Bulk downloads, printing or uploads to personal storage after notice
Access to material unrelated to handover
Forwarding work email to personal accounts
Deleting files or changing passwords on shared resources

controls.screening: Not applicable.
controls.privileged_access: Reduce privileges at notice; remove admin rights before an adverse separation is announced.
controls.separation_of_duties: Handover is supervised by the manager, not done alone.
controls.monitoring: A defined, disclosed look-back and look-forward window around departure, with HR notifying security at notice.
controls.offboarding: Same-day revocation, asset recovery, exit interview covering continuing obligations, and retained access to the person's data for the organization.

roles.name: People changing roles or teams

why.access: Old access is often kept while new access is added.
why.trust: Accumulated access is rarely questioned.
why.opportunity: Combinations of access that no single role should hold, breaking separation of duties.
why.pressure: Usually none; this is a control gap more than a behavior risk.

typical_access: Union of every role the person has held
indicators: Entitlements from a previous role still in use
Access combinations that break separation of duties

controls.screening: Rescreen if the new role carries a higher designation.
controls.privileged_access: Review and remove prior-role access at transfer.
controls.separation_of_duties: Check the new combination against separation-of-duties rules.
controls.monitoring: Access recertification by the new manager.
controls.offboarding: Not applicable.

categories.name: Financial institutions
categories.summary: Banks and credit unions add roles with direct access to member or customer money and data. Section 205(d) and its bank equivalent already bar some people from these institutions entirely.

roles.name: Tellers, branch staff and vault custodians

why.access: Cash, negotiable instruments and account maintenance at the point of service.
why.trust: Trusted with cash every day and with members' identity documents.
why.opportunity: Cash theft, unauthorized withdrawals from dormant or elderly members' accounts, and helping outsiders open fraudulent accounts.
why.pressure: Lower pay, personal financial strain, and recruitment by organized fraud rings.

indicators: Cash differences that recur
Transactions on dormant accounts
Address or phone changes followed by withdrawals
Overrides requested from the same supervisor repeatedly

controls.screening: Section 205(d) or Section 19 checks as required, plus standard screening.
controls.privileged_access: Override and maintenance rights limited and logged.
controls.separation_of_duties: Dual control on vaults and high-value transactions.
controls.monitoring: Teller differences, override and dormant-account monitoring; mandatory time away.
controls.offboarding: Balance and recover cash and keys; revoke core access.

roles.name: Loan officers, underwriters and loan servicing

why.access: Credit decisions, collateral records and loan modifications.
why.trust: Trusted to apply credit policy and to waive or modify terms.
why.opportunity: Fraudulent loans to associates or straw borrowers, kickbacks, and hiding delinquencies.
why.pressure: Production incentives and relationships with borrowers or brokers.

indicators: Loans to related parties without disclosure
Repeated policy exceptions for the same broker or borrower group
Modifications or extensions that hide delinquency

controls.screening: Section 205(d) or Section 19 checks plus elevated screening for lenders with approval authority.
controls.privileged_access: Lending limits by role; exceptions above limits require a second approver.
controls.separation_of_duties: Origination, underwriting approval and funding by different people.
controls.monitoring: Related-party and exception reporting; loan review sampling.
controls.offboarding: Review the officer's recent approvals and exceptions.

roles.name: Fraud operations and BSA/AML analysts

why.access: Fraud and AML alerts, investigation files, and in some cases authority to release holds or close alerts.
why.trust: Trusted to recognize and stop financial crime.
why.opportunity: Clearing alerts for collaborators, tipping off subjects, or leaking SAR-related information.
why.pressure: High alert volumes and targeting by the criminals they work against.

indicators: Alerts on connected parties closed by the same analyst
Threshold or rule changes without review
Case lookups with no assigned alert

controls.screening: Elevated screening; Section 205(d) or Section 19 checks.
controls.privileged_access: Rule and threshold changes restricted and logged.
controls.separation_of_duties: Quality review of closed alerts by someone else; no one works alerts involving people they know.
controls.monitoring: Audit case access and alert dispositions.
controls.offboarding: Reassign open cases under supervision.

roles.name: Contact center agents with account access

why.access: Look up and change member or customer accounts, often in high volume and remotely.
why.trust: Trusted to verify callers and act on their behalf.
why.opportunity: Selling account data, enabling account takeover by changing contact details or resetting credentials, and SIM-swap-style collusion.
why.pressure: Lower pay, high turnover, and active recruitment by fraud groups, including through social media.

indicators: Lookups on accounts with no matching inbound contact
Contact or credential changes followed by fraud
Screen capture or photos of screens in remote settings

controls.screening: Section 205(d) or Section 19 checks plus standard screening.
controls.privileged_access: Account access tied to an active contact; high-risk changes require step-up verification.
controls.separation_of_duties: High-risk changes reviewed or confirmed out of band.
controls.monitoring: Lookup-without-contact analytics and linkage to downstream fraud.
controls.offboarding: Revoke access at end of shift on notice; collect remote equipment.

categories.name: Healthcare and clinical
categories.summary: Included briefly because many practitioners support hospitals and health plans; the same reasoning extends further.

roles.name: Clinical and administrative staff with EHR access

why.access: Patient records, often with broad break-the-glass access for emergencies.
why.trust: Trusted to look only at patients they care for.
why.opportunity: Snooping on celebrities, colleagues or family, and selling records for identity or insurance fraud.
why.pressure: Burnout and personal curiosity; outside offers for records.

indicators: Records opened with no care relationship
Same-surname or VIP record access
Break-the-glass use without a matching event

controls.screening: Workforce clearance procedure under the HIPAA Security Rule.
controls.privileged_access: Role-based EHR access with break-the-glass logged and reviewed.
controls.separation_of_duties: Billing changes and record corrections reviewed.
controls.monitoring: Regular review of information system activity, including access-pattern analytics.
controls.offboarding: Termination procedures that end ePHI access promptly.

roles.name: Pharmacy and staff with access to controlled substances

why.access: Controlled substance stock, dispensing cabinets and records.
why.trust: Trusted to handle and record drugs with diversion value.
why.opportunity: Diversion for personal use or sale, and falsifying waste or count records.
why.pressure: Substance use disorder, which calls for a clinical and supportive response as well as a security one.

indicators: Dispensing or waste patterns well above peers
Waste without a witness
Count discrepancies on the same shifts

controls.screening: Registrants may not employ certain people in roles with controlled substance access under 21 CFR 1301.76.
controls.privileged_access: Cabinet access by role and unit.
controls.separation_of_duties: Witnessed waste and independent counts.
controls.monitoring: Diversion analytics on dispensing data; theft or significant loss reported to DEA within one business day.
controls.offboarding: Revoke cabinet and vault access immediately.
